title: Space Force Pays Rocket Lab $397 Million to Build 'Flatellites' That Track Threats
summary:
Did you know that satellites can be flat? That's the idea behind Rocket Lab's new 'Flatellites.' The U.S. Space Force just gave the company $397 million to build a bunch of them. These flat satellites will help track enemy planes and missiles in real time.

Why flat? Because flat satellites can be stacked together like pancakes, so more of them can fit on one rocket. That means we can launch more satellites at once, which is great for building a big network in space.

The Flatellites will be part of the Space Force's plan to keep an eye on the sky. They'll have special sensors and communication systems to spot threats. They'll launch on Rocket Lab's new Neutron rocket, which is like a big brother to their smaller Electron rocket. Neutron is expected to fly for the first time later this year or in early 2027.

This isn't Rocket Lab's first big space contract. Since the beginning of 2026, they've signed four major deals with the U.S. government worth a total of $943 million. That includes launching missile-defense missions from Alaska and testing hypersonic rockets.

Rocket Lab's CEO, Peter Beck, is excited. He says they've 'mastered the art of building launch sites' and are now making them portable. They even have a new system called GHOST that can launch rockets from shipping containers, so they can go anywhere in the world.

This is a big deal for space technology. Flat satellites could change how we build and launch spacecraft. And with all these new contracts, Rocket Lab is becoming a major player in space defense. Who knows what they'll build next?
why_it_matters: Satellites built for defense can lead to new space technology that might one day improve GPS, weather forecasts, and communication you use every day.
